modules.name: Energy Band Theory and Classification of Materials

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
Electronics: The word "electronics' is derived from electron+dynamics which means the study of the behaviour of an electron under different conditions of externally applied fields.

Main application of electronics is computer which in used in every field.

All electronics equipment required D.C. supply for operation (not A.C. supply).

Energy band: Energy bands refer to the range of energy levels that electrons can occupy in a solid. These bands form when atomic orbitals overlap in a crystal lattice.

Types of energy bands

1. Valence Band: The highest range of electron energies where electrons are present at absolute zero temperature.

2. Conduction Band: The range of energies where electrons are free to move and contribute to electrical conduction. Electrons in this band are not bound to atoms and can move through the material.

3. Forbidden band (or band gap energy):- The energy difference between the valence band and the conduction band.

$\Delta \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{g}}=(\mathrm{CB})_{\min }-(\mathrm{VB})_{\max }$

  • Width of forbidden energy gap depends upon the nature of substance.
  • Width is more, then valence electrons are strongly attached with nucleus.
  • Width of forbidden energy gap is represented in eV.
  • As temperature increases forbidden energy gap decreases (very slightly).

blocks.question:

(2) current in p-type > current in n-type

(3) current in n-type > current in p-type

blocks.answer:
(3) current in n-type > current in p-type

In N type semiconductor majority charge carriers are e and P type semiconductor majority charge carriers are holes.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{neA} v_d=\operatorname{neA}(\mu \mathrm{E}) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu_e>\mu_h \Rightarrow \quad I_e>I_h$

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
P-N Junction Diode & Diode Formation:

When a P-type semiconductor is joined to a N-type semiconductor such that the crystal structure remains continuous at the boundary, the resulting arrangement is called a P-N junction diode.

There are two important processes in the p-n junction.

1. Diffusion: It occurs for majority charge carriers due to concentration gradient. Holes diffuses from p-side to n-side of the junction. Electrons diffuses from n-side to p-side of the junction. Direction of diffusion current is from p-side to n-side.

2. Drift: It occurs for minority charge carriers due to electric field in the depletion region. Electron drift from p-side to the n-side of the junction. Holes drift from n-side to the p-side of the junction. Electrons and holes drift to their respective majority sides. Direction of drift current is from n to p, opposite to that of diffusion current.

• Thus, a p-n junction is formed. In a p-n junction under equilibrium there is no net current. It means

$\left|I_{\text {Drift }}\right|=\left|I_{\text {Diffusion }}\right|$

(At equilibrium condition)

Depletion Width:

Width of Depletion region $ \approx 0.1 \mu \mathrm{~m}$

It depends on temperature, doping and type of material width

$ \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text { Doping }}}$

Barrier Potential: An electric field forms from the n-side to the p-side, with the n-region having a higher potential. The potential difference across the junction creates a barrier that prevents the movement of majority carriers (electrons and holes), known as the "potential barrier." This barrier depends on temperature, doping, and the semiconductor material, opposing majority carrier motion while allowing minority carriers to move.

Types of Biasing

1. Forward Biasing:- p-side  is connected to the positive terminal and n-side to the negative terminal.

2. Reverse Biasing:- n-side  is connected to the positive terminal and p-side to the negative terminal

Breakdown voltage : It is the reverse voltage at which a diode starts conducting heavily in the reverse direction, usually causing damage if exceeded.

Breakdown : When the reverse voltage exceeds a certain limit, causing the diode to conduct in the reverse direction.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Rectifier:- It converts alternating current into direct current. It can be used as a rectifier since it is a uni-directional device.

(A) Half Wave Rectifier : A half-wave rectifier is an electronic circuit that converts alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC) by allowing only one half (positive or negative) of the AC waveform to pass through, while blocking the other half. This results in a pulsating DC output. It typically uses a single diode for the rectification process.

(B) Full-wave Rectifier (Centre Tap Full Wave Rectifier):A full-wave rectifier is an electronic circuit that converts the entire AC waveform into DC by utilizing both the positive and negative halves of the AC signal. It typically uses two or four diodes to achieve this, providing a smoother and more efficient DC output compared to a half-wave rectifier.

(C) Bridge Rectifier : A bridge rectifier is a type of full-wave rectifier that uses four diodes arranged in a bridge configuration to convert AC to DC. It allows both halves of the AC waveform to be used, providing a smoother and more efficient DC output without the need for a center-tapped transformer.

Rectifier efficiency:

1. For Half Wave Rectifier:  $\eta_{\max }=40.6 \%$

2. For Full Wave Rectifier: $\eta_{\max }=81.2 \%$

Ripple Frequency:  The frequency of the fluctuations (ripples) in the output of a rectifier circuit.

Filter Circuit : Circuits designed to remove unwanted components, such as ripple, from a rectified signal and smooth the output.

Capacitor Filter : A capacitor filter  charges to the peak voltage of the rectified output when there is no load. With a load, it discharges, but in the next cycle, it recharges to the peak value. Due to the capacitor's large time constant, the voltage across it remains nearly constant, smoothing the output.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question: A half-wave rectifier is connected to an AC supply of 230 V (rms). The diode drop is negligible. Calculate the average (DC) output voltage.
blocks.answer:
Answer: $V_{d c} \approx 103.6 \mathrm{~V}$

Explanation:

$\text { Input peak voltage } V_m=\sqrt{2} \times V_{r m s}=\sqrt{2} \times 230=325.27 \mathrm{~V}$

Average output voltage for half-wave rectifier:

$\displaystyle V_{d c}=\frac{V_m}{\pi}=\frac{325.27}{3.1416}=103.6 \mathrm{~V}$

$V_{d c} \approx 103.6 \mathrm{~V}$

blocks.title: Electronic Devices
blocks.text:
1. Zener Diode : Special purpose diode invented by C. Zener. Heavily doped P-N junction. Works like a normal diode in forward bias. Mainly operated in reverse bias breakdown region.

Symbol of Zener Diode:

I-V characteristic:

Zener diode as a voltage regulator : Regulation is possible because, in the breakdown region, the Zener voltage remains constant despite changes in current. When the input voltage increases, the current through the Zener diode and series resistor (RS) increases, and vice versa. This causes a change in the voltage drop across RS, but the voltage across the load remains unchanged, allowing the Zener diode to act as a voltage regulator.

Load voltage is constant and load current is also constant $ \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$

$\text { Input current is, } \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{z}}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{s}}}$

$\text { Zener Current } \mathrm{I}_Z=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{S}}-\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{L}}$

$P_Z=V_Z I_Z$

2. Light Emitting Diode (L.E.D) : A Light Emitting Diode converts electrical current into light. LEDs are heavily doped p-n junctions and operated under forward bias. Outer material must be transparent so that photons can escape.

  • An LED works by allowing current to flow from the anode to the cathode. When forward biased, electrons move from the N-side to the P-side, where they recombine with holes. This recombination releases energy in the form of photons, producing light. The intensity of the light depends on the forward current, with maximum brightness at a certain current level.
3. Photodiode : A photo-diode converts light into electrical current or voltage. Photo-diode are moderately doped p-n junctions and operated under reverse bias. Outer material must be transparent so that photons can enter.

When light with energy greater than the band gap strikes a photodiode, it moves electrons from the valence to conduction band, increasing current in reverse bias. As light intensity rises, the photocurrent increases. Photodiodes are used to detect light intensity, such as in video cameras.

4. Solar Cell : It converts light energy into electrical energy. It has same working principle as that of photo-diode but working method is different. It is operated unbiased. The surface layer of p-region is made very thin so that the incident photons may easily penetrate to reach the junction which is the active region.

A solar cell works by converting light energy into electrical energy. When sunlight strikes the cell, it excites electrons in the semiconductor material, creating electron-hole pairs. These charge carriers are separated by the electric field at the p-n junction, generating a flow of current that can be used as electricity.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Discuss the impact of temperature on solar cell efficiency.
blocks.answer: Solar cell efficiency decreases with increasing temperature. This is due to an increase in the reverse saturation current and a decrease in the open-circuit voltage.
blocks.prompt: Discuss the impact of temperature on solar cell efficiency.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: How does the color of an LED affect its forward voltage and efficiency?
blocks.answer: The forward voltage of an LED increases as the emitted wavelength decreases (i.e., from red to blue). The efficiency can also vary depending on the material and manufacturing process.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not constructing the correct truth table for a given logic gate or circuit.
  • Confusing gates like NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR, etc.
  • Mixing up the symbols or operators in Boolean algebra.
  • Overcomplicating Boolean expressions without simplifying them.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misunderstanding Doping Effects: Incorrectly identifying n-type and p-type materials.
    • Confusing Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors: Mixing up pure and doped semiconductors.
    • Ignoring Temperature Effects: Not considering how temperature affects conductivity.
    • Misapplying Energy Bands: Incorrectly identifying conduction and valence bands or the band gap.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing Forward and Reverse Bias: Incorrectly predicting current flow direction.
    • Ignoring Threshold Voltage: Forgetting the diode's cut-in voltage (0.7V for silicon).
    • Misusing the Diode Equation: Incorrect application of the diode current equation.
    • Overlooking Reverse Breakdown: Ignoring breakdown voltage in reverse bias.
    • Misunderstanding Diode Applications: Errors in analyzing diodes in rectifiers or other circuits.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Choosing a transformer with an incorrect voltage or current rating
  • Diodes must be installed with the correct polarity
  • The DC output of rectifiers often contains ripples.
